title: evolutionary-biology Mindmap
notes: The origin of life is explained by chemical evolution (abiogenesis). The Oparin-Haldane theory proposed that a reducing early atmosphere allowed inorganic…
Origin of life: life arose from non-living matter by chemical evolution (abiogenesis) in a warm dilution (primordial ocean).
Oparin-Haldane theory (1924/29): the early reducing atmosphere (CH4, NH3, H2O, H2, no O2) allowed formation of organic molecules from inorganic ones.

subtopics.name: Key points
points: Oparin-Haldane: reducing early atmosphere allowed chemical evolution.
Stages: simple organics → polymers → coacervates → self-replicating systems.
Miller-Urey (1953): produced amino acids from inorganic precursors.
RNA world: self-replicating, catalytic RNA may predate DNA/protein life.
Abiogenesis (origin of life) ≠ spontaneous generation (disproved).

subtopics.name: Formulas & relations
points: Chemical evolution: Inorganic (CH4, NH3, H2O, H2) → Simple organics (amino acids, sugars, bases) → Polymers…
Miller-Urey: electric sparks (lightning) + reducing atmosphere → amino acids

subtopics.name: Statements to quote
points: Life arose from non-living matter through gradual chemical evolution.
The Miller-Urey experiment provided experimental support for chemical evolution.
The early Earth atmosphere was reducing and oxygen-free.

subtopics.name: Exam focus
points: Explain the Oparin-Haldane theory with 4 stages.
Describe the Miller-Urey experiment (setup, conditions, results).
What is the RNA world hypothesis?
Oparin-Haldane = O-H (Organics from Heat).
Miller-Urey = M-U (Made Urea... no — Made amino acids from Urey's setup).

The early atmosphere was reducing (no free O2); free oxygen came later from photosynthetic cyanobacteria.

subtopics.name: Key points
points: Five types of evidence: morphological, anatomical, fossil, embryological, biochemical.
Homologous (divergent) vs analogous (convergent) organs.
Vestigial organs = reduced ancestral remnants.
Fossils show progressive complexity; transitional forms link groups.
Embryos of vertebrates are similar early, diverge later.

subtopics.name: Formulas & relations
points: Homologous: same structure, different function, common origin (divergent evolution)
Analogous: different structure, same function, different origin (convergent evolution)
Vestigial: reduced remnant of an ancestral organ
Molecular: DNA/protein similarity inversely related to evolutionary distance

subtopics.name: Statements to quote
points: Homologous structures indicate common descent with divergent evolution.
Analogous structures result from convergent evolution under similar selection pressures.
Vestigial organs are remnants of structures that were functional in ancestors.

subtopics.name: Exam focus
points: Differentiate homologous and analogous organs (with examples).
Explain vestigial organs as evidence of evolution.
Describe the significance of Archaeopteryx.
Homo = same origin; Ana = same function.
Vestigial = "Vest" (a leftover vest of evolution).

subtopics.name: Common misconceptions
points: Homologous = same origin, different function (divergent); Analogous = different origin, same function…
Vestigial organs are evidence of common ancestry, not of "uselessness" in an absolute sense.
Fossils are not just "old bones"; they include traces (footprints, burrows), impressions, and molecular…

subtopics.name: Key points
points: Lamarckism: use/disuse + inheritance of acquired traits (rejected).
Darwinism: natural selection; variation, overproduction, survival of fittest.
Neo-Darwinism: genetics + selection + drift + gene flow + recombination.
Evolution = change in allele frequencies in a population.
Natural selection is non-random; genetic drift is random.

subtopics.name: Formulas & relations
points: Hardy-Weinberg: p² + 2pq + q² = 1 (p = dominant allele freq, q = recessive)
Natural selection: variation → struggle → survival of fittest → adaptation
Evolution (modern): change in allele frequencies in a population over generations

subtopics.name: Statements to quote
points: Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characteristics lacks a hereditary mechanism and is largely rejected.
Darwin's natural selection explains adaptation through variation and differential survival.
Neo-Darwinism (modern synthesis) explains evolution as change in allele frequencies.

subtopics.name: Exam focus
points: Compare Lamarckism and Darwinism (postulates, example, status).
Describe the modern synthesis (Neo-Darwinism).
Differentiate natural selection from genetic drift.
Lamarck = L-A-M (Learned, Acquired, Modified) traits — inherited (wrong).
Darwin = D-N-S (Difference, Nature, Selection) — survival of the fittest.

subtopics.name: Key points
points: Humans: Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Mammalia, Order Primates, Family Hominidae.
Primates: grasping hands, forward eyes, large brain.
New World (Platyrrhini) vs Old World (Cercopithecinae) monkeys.
Apes (no tail): gorilla, chimpanzee, orangutan, gibbon, humans (hominids).
Human evolution: bipedalism → tool use → fire → brain enlargement → language.

subtopics.name: Formulas & relations
points: Taxonomic position: Animalia > Chordata > Mammalia > Primates > Hominidae > Homo > Homo sapiens
Evolutionary sequence: Australopithecus → H. habilis → H. erectus → H. neanderthalensis → H. sapiens
Key adaptations: bipedalism, encephalisation, language, culture

subtopics.name: Statements to quote
points: Humans are primates in the family Hominidae.
Bipedalism evolved before the large brain in human ancestors.
The sequence Australopithecus → H. habilis → H. erectus → H. sapiens is well supported by fossils.

subtopics.name: Exam focus
points: State the taxonomic position of humans.
Differentiate New World and Old World monkeys.
Describe the main features of Australopithecus, H. habilis, and H. erectus.
Human = H-O-M-O (Homo sapiens) = Mammal + Primate + Hominid.
Apes = no tail; Monkeys = tail (usually).

subtopics.name: Common misconceptions
points: Humans are NOT apes; we are hominids (great apes) within the family Hominidae, but a distinct lineage.
Australopithecus was bipedal but had a small brain (~400–500 mL); the brain enlarged later in Homo.
